summary: Use outside design lessons as a small boost on top of your own experience, skill and way of thinking, and keep the shared goal in view: making games a little more fun.
takeaways: Goal: help make games around the world a little more fun
Lessons are a boost; your own experience is the foundation
Explain basics simply, even what the field considers common knowledge
Keep each lesson bite-sized, 2-5 minutes, so it is retained

principles.principle: Explain design ideas simply, in short bite-sized units
principles.why: He keeps things simple so people without development experience can follow, and keeps each video to 2-5 minutes because the longer he talks, the harder it is to retain everything.
principles.how: When briefing or teaching, spell out even 'common knowledge' concepts and split topics into short units.
principles.anti_pattern: Long, technical explanations that assume expert knowledge.
principles.quote: In fact, I think keeping things simple is for the best.

principles.principle: Treat outside advice as a boost to your own judgment
principles.why: He says the foundation is the viewer's own experience, skill and way of thinking; his videos only give a little extra boost, and your mileage may vary.
principles.how: Use design lessons to sharpen judgment built by making and playing games, rather than as rules to follow blindly.
principles.quote: The foundation is the viewer's experience, skill, and way of thinking.

summary: Be able to sum up each game in one line that says who it is for or what its hook is, the way every one of Sakurai's works is captioned here.
takeaways: Each of his works is summed up in one caption
Captions name the audience or the signature hook
Works span Kirby, Smash Bros., Meteos, columns, concerts, toys

principles.principle: Sum up your game in one line: its audience or hook
principles.why: Inferred from the episode's format, not stated: every work is captioned with one line naming who it is for ('tailor-made for newcomers', 'beginners and pros alike') or its signature mechanic ('copy enemy abilities', 'smash foes off the screen').
principles.how: Write a one-sentence pitch naming your target player or core hook and check it reads clearly as a caption.
principles.example: Kirby's Adventure caption: 'A fun romp for beginners and pros alike that introduced the power to copy enemy abilities.'
principles.quote: A fun romp for beginners and pros alike that introduced the power to copy enemy abilities.

summary: Briefly stop the action at your game's big moments (landing a hit, beating a boss, getting hit or dying) so players clearly feel the impact of their success or defeat.
takeaways: Hit stop completely changes how heavy a hit feels
Stop and flash the screen when a boss is defeated
Freeze the moment the player is hit so impact is clear
Layer stop, screen shake and slow motion for big moments
Stops are easy to implement, so use them everywhere

principles.principle: Add hit stop so attacks feel heavy
principles.why: A brief stop in the action when a hit lands completely changes how heavy the hit feels.
principles.how: Freeze the action for a brief moment when an attack connects, and compare with and without it.
principles.anti_pattern: Skimping on stop effects as minor polish.
principles.quote: Whether or not it's there will completely change how heavy a hit feels, so it's a pretty important effect.

principles.principle: Stop and flash the screen when a boss is defeated
principles.why: His 'boss stop' is vital for letting the player really feel the impact of beating a boss.
principles.how: On boss defeat, freeze the screen and flash it for a moment before the defeat sequence plays.
principles.example: Kirby's Adventure (NES) boss defeats; Super Smash Bros. Ultimate's Finish Zoom extends the idea.
principles.quote: When you defeat a boss, the screen stops and flashes for a moment. This is vital for letting the player really feel that impact.

principles.principle: Freeze the action when the player gets hit or dies
principles.why: In many scrolling shoot 'em ups players die without realizing; 'Wait, I got hit?' only tells them something is wrong, which is a missed opportunity. A pause shows the point of impact and gives an 'oh no!' feeling.
principles.how: Pause the game for an instant when the player takes damage or loses a life so the point of impact is visible.
principles.anti_pattern: Letting players die without seeing what happened.
principles.example: Fantasy Zone (1986) stops the screen for a second on hit; Defender (1980) builds a stop into its hit effect.
principles.quote: The takeaway shouldn't be, "Wait, I got hit?" That just tells you that something's wrong.

principles.principle: Layer stop, shake and slow motion at big moments
principles.why: Stopping is one of many tools, and these effects let players feel moments of success or defeat; they are relatively easy to implement.
principles.how: For the biggest moments, combine a screen stop with screen shake and slow motion.
principles.example: Shooting-game footage shown with no effects, then with stop, shake and slow motion added.
principles.quote: In your game's big moments, stop! Let your players feel those moments of success—or defeat.

summary: Decide who your game is for and shape its risks to match, as Kirby's Dream Land cut risk on purpose (inhale enemies, fly over pits) to welcome newcomers and relied on fun worth replaying, not punishing difficulty, for long-term value.
takeaways: Core idea: let the player use enemies, not just beat them
Flight exists because losing a life for a missed jump felt harsh
Deliberately reduced risk to welcome newcomers
Get replay value from fun, not unreasonable difficulty
Music was tied into stage starts and the victory dance

principles.principle: Lower risks deliberately when targeting newcomers
principles.why: He wanted the first Kirby to be as accessible as possible for new players; inhaling enemies and flying both reduced the risks players faced, and he kept going despite staff asking 'Are you sure about this?'
principles.how: Give players tools that cut risk (fly over pits, neutralize enemies) while keeping some penalty, such as losing a life if you do fall.
principles.anti_pattern: Making games unreasonably hard, which leaves beginners out in the cold.
principles.example: Kirby's Dream Land: inhale-and-spit and flight.
principles.quote: Inhaling enemies and flying both reduced the potential risks players faced during gameplay.

principles.principle: Let players use enemies, not only defeat them
principles.why: He found it fun for the player to use enemies, because of risk and reward and the dual purpose enemies serve; Mega Man's boss weapons are a reward for winning, not using the enemies.
principles.how: Give the player a simple way to turn on-screen enemies into tools, such as inhaling and spitting them out.
principles.example: Kirby's Dream Land inhale (a tongue grab was the first idea) vs. Mega Man boss weapons.
principles.quote: I just thought it would be fun if the player could use enemies.

principles.principle: Don't punish minor mistakes like missed jumps with instant death
principles.why: Being hit and missing a jump are not serious mistakes, yet even games with health bars made falling an instant death; he thought losing a life for a missed jump was too harsh.
principles.how: Keep a penalty for falling but give players a way to recover, such as the ability to fly over gaps.
principles.anti_pattern: Treating every small slip as the harshest failure.
principles.example: Kirby's Dream Land flight.
principles.quote: I gave him the ability to fly because I thought it was too harsh to lose a life just for missing a jump.

principles.principle: Earn replay value through fun, not unreasonable difficulty
principles.why: Limited NES cartridge memory pushed games to be tough so players wouldn't finish too quickly, but unreasonable difficulty shut out beginners; like arcade games, a fun game gets played again and again.
principles.how: Aim for play that feels good to repeat rather than padding a short game with punishing difficulty.
principles.anti_pattern: Using difficulty as a substitute for content.
principles.example: NES-era hard games vs. Kirby's Dream Land.
principles.quote: If it's fun, you'll play it again and again.

summary: Treat frames as your game's unit of time (distance = time × speed), and choose your frame rate on purpose: 60 fps is ideal, 30 fps is an acceptable standard.
takeaways: Frames are a unit of time: distance = time × speed
60 fps is ideal; 30 fps is an acceptable standard
60 fps costs half your visual performance
A variable frame rate is not the same as slowdown
PAL ports ran 5/6 speed when time counted screen interrupts

principles.principle: Treat frames as your unit of time when tuning motion
principles.why: In games, frames are often the unit of time, and since distance = time × speed, time has a huge effect on how far and fast things move.
principles.how: Specify movement and action timings in frames at your target frame rate and tune speeds with that in mind.
principles.quote: In games, these frames are often used as a unit of time. Distance = Time × Speed.

principles.principle: Target 60 fps when possible; accept 30 fps when visuals need it
principles.why: 60 and 30 fps differ in look and in how smoothly they control; drawing twice as many frames sacrifices half your visual performance, and 30 fps is still more than adequate.
principles.how: Choose the target frame rate early by weighing control smoothness against the rendering budget.
principles.example: Side-by-side 60 fps vs. 30 fps footage.
principles.quote: 60 fps is an ideal frame rate when possible, but 30 fps is also a common standard.

principles.principle: Keep game speed independent of how many frames are drawn
principles.why: His NES/SNES games counted screen interrupts as time, so 50 fps PAL versions ran 5/6 as fast; from the N64 on, drawing fewer frames while running as intended caused less jarring tradeoffs. Dropping frames is not slowdown.
principles.how: Decouple game logic timing from display refresh so frame drops or regional refresh rates don't change game speed.
principles.anti_pattern: Tying game speed to a refresh rate that differs by region or platform.
principles.example: NES/SNES PAL ports at 5/6 speed.
principles.quote: In other words, porting games to PAL caused them to run 5/6 as fast.

summary: Build your core fun from risk and reward placed close together in the right amounts, so the moment of greatest danger is also the moment the player can win something.
takeaways: Game essence is push and pull: take risks to get rewards
Strategy is how players manage risk to get rewards
Place risk and reward close together, in the right amounts
Hitbox size is a balance lever, not just visual design
More game essence narrows a game's broad appeal

principles.principle: Put risk and reward close together, in the right amounts
principles.why: Fun comes from taking risks to get rewards; in Super Mario Bros. the highest-risk moment, right next to the Koopa Troopa, is the only time you can beat it.
principles.how: Design core interactions so the player must enter danger to score, and attach new risk to rewards, like a kicked shell that can bounce back.
principles.anti_pattern: Rewards with no attached risk.
principles.example: Space Invaders: you can only hit an invader from where it can hit you. Super Mario Bros.: stomping a Koopa Troopa, then kicking its shell.
principles.quote: Take risks to get rewards. This push and pull is the very core of game essence.

principles.principle: Tune player hitbox size as a core balance parameter
principles.why: In Space Invaders the cannon's width determines how great your risk is; a different size could change how deep and engaging the game is. Mechanics that vary risk, like hiding halfway under a bunker, also matter.
principles.how: Treat character size, hitboxes and partial cover as levers that set how risky approaching is, and tune them deliberately.
principles.anti_pattern: Treating character size as purely visual design.
principles.example: Space Invaders cannon width and bunkers.
principles.quote: Your cannon's width is key to game balance because it determines how great your risk is.

principles.principle: Don't add powerful options that erase risk without counterweights
principles.why: A three-way laser in Space Invaders might look cool but probably wouldn't be good design, unless enemies also shot diagonally or ammo were limited.
principles.how: Before adding a strong option, check what risk it removes and counterbalance it, for example with limited ammo.
principles.anti_pattern: Cool-looking power-ups that remove the push and pull.
principles.example: Hypothetical three-way laser in Space Invaders.
principles.quote: Imagine how Space Invaders would feel with a three-way laser. It might look cool, but it probably wouldn't be the best game design.

principles.principle: Dial game essence down for a broad audience
principles.why: His theory is that as you increase game essence, you reduce a game's broad appeal; he made the first Kirby deliberately simpler to reach a wider audience.
principles.how: Decide how much push and pull your target audience wants and simplify for wide audiences.
principles.anti_pattern: Assuming more depth is always better for everyone.
principles.example: Kirby's Dream Land, made deliberately simpler.
principles.quote: As you increase "game essence," you reduce a game's broad appeal.

summary: Approach game development as a professional job: set your personal taste aside, find the fun in whatever genre or goal you're given, and never lose sight of entertaining players.
takeaways: Game development is a job, not a game
Pros respond to demand, indie developers included
Set personal taste aside; design to the assignment's goal
Understanding fun lets you make any kind of game
When lost, remember the goal: entertain players

principles.principle: Treat paid game development as a job, not a hobby
principles.why: Once money, sales and numbers are involved, development is a job like any other; indie developers become professionals too, and being a pro means being light on your feet and responding to demand.
principles.how: Do assigned work well even when it isn't to your taste, and look for what makes it interesting and rewarding.
principles.anti_pattern: Only working on what you personally enjoy once you're paid.
principles.example: An artist who loves cute things texturing lifelike zombies and roaches.
principles.quote: The job of a game developer is to create games, but the work itself is not a game.

principles.principle: Design to the assignment's genre and goal, not your own taste
principles.why: He made Kirby's Dream Land for newcomers despite being an experienced gamer and Meteos despite not being good at block puzzles; once you understand what makes games fun, you can create any kind of experience.
principles.how: Write down the genre, goal and audience each project must fit, then find the fun within that brief.
principles.anti_pattern: Designing games for yourself.
principles.example: Kirby's Dream Land; Meteos.
principles.quote: I view every project that comes my way as an assignment in which I create a game to fit a certain genre or goal.

principles.principle: When you lose your way, return to entertaining players
principles.why: Every developer shares one goal, entertaining players, and that desire supplies the motivation to keep going through development's challenges.
principles.how: When stuck or demotivated, ask how the decision in front of you entertains the player and choose accordingly.
principles.quote: If you feel like you've lost your way, just remember: entertain players.

summary: Your game's responsiveness is only as good as the player's display and audio setup, so learn to recognize input lag and test and demo on screens set to Game Mode or Low Latency Mode with extra processing turned off.
takeaways: Many people don't recognize input lag when they see it
Test lag by pressing jump in an instant-response NES game
Use Game Mode/Low Latency Mode; disable picture processing
Audio can lag separately through home theater systems
At 60 fps, 16.67 ms of delay is one frame

principles.principle: Check input lag on every demo and test setup yourself
principles.why: At E3 2018 the setup crew must have tested Smash Ultimate, yet nobody noticed lag bad enough to ruin the controls; many people don't recognize lag.
principles.how: Press jump in a game that responds instantly (an NES game, not a 3D one) on the actual setup and confirm the character moves the moment you press.
principles.anti_pattern: Assuming a setup is fine because someone else already played on it.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate at E3 2018 Treehouse: Live.
principles.quote: Even though the setup crew must have tested the game out before the event, nobody noticed the lag.

principles.principle: Use Game Mode and disable picture processing on displays
principles.why: Display latency comes from post-processing that improves picture quality; Game Mode or Low Latency Mode bypasses it. At 60 fps every 16.67 ms is a frame of delay.
principles.how: Switch test and play TVs to Game Mode or Low Latency Mode, or turn off all picture-enhancing settings, and prefer TVs with low listed display time.
principles.anti_pattern: Leaving TV post-processing on for gameplay.
principles.quote: With a 60 fps video output, a delay of 16.67 ms equates to one frame.

principles.principle: Check audio latency separately from video
principles.why: Sometimes only the sound is delayed; through a home theater system you might hear impact sounds a little late.
principles.how: Use an analog audio connection or low-latency audio settings, and experiment if equipment doesn't get along.
principles.quote: If you're using a home theater system, you might hear the impact sounds a little late.

summary: Put players under stress with enemies, obstacles or puzzles, then release it, and reward their success with choices that help them handle the next, bigger squeeze.
takeaways: Games stress players to provide relief; that's core fun
Stress can be any enemy, obstacle or puzzle impeding progress
Reward success with better ways to relieve future stress
Choice in rewards boosts game essence
Ask why other games do things before copying them

principles.principle: Squeeze players with stress, then release it
principles.why: Stress alone isn't fun, but heavy pressure followed by sudden release brings great satisfaction; a game with no stress probably wouldn't be much fun.
principles.how: Put an enemy, obstacle or puzzle in the way of progress, then let the player overcome it.
principles.anti_pattern: Weeding stress out entirely.
principles.quote: Stress on its own isn't fun, but if you really squeeze a player, then whoosh! set them free, it can bring great satisfaction.

principles.principle: Reward cleared challenges with choices that prepare for the next
principles.why: Release is just the first step; rewards should give new ways to relieve stress more effectively, and providing choice boosts game essence.
principles.how: After each challenge, grant EXP, new skills or currency for equipment, and let the player choose how to use them.
principles.anti_pattern: Rewards that are only linear progress with no choice.
principles.example: Experience points, new skills, currency for better equipment.
principles.quote: Apply stress, allow for release, and prepare players for what's next.

principles.principle: Ask why other games do something before copying it
principles.why: Reexamining why other games do things, instead of mimicking them, boosts your chances of making something fresh and innovative.
principles.how: Before borrowing a mechanic, write down why it works in its source game and whether that reason applies to yours.
principles.anti_pattern: Mimicking other games' features without understanding them.
principles.quote: Don't just mimic the things other games are doing. Reexamine why they do them, and you'll boost your chances of making something fresh and innovative.

summary: Don't call an asset finished once it's modeled and textured; finish it by showing the light it reflects in its environment, using cheap techniques like colored light, hue variation and atmosphere.
takeaways: Don't draw the asset; draw the light it reflects
Base colors alone don't finish an asset
Colored light, hue variation and atmosphere bring scenes alive
Prefer simple techniques so more objects fit on screen

principles.principle: Draw the light an asset reflects, not just the asset
principles.why: Everything we see is light reflected into our eyes, not simply 'a red thing as red'; an asset textured with base colors (brown trunk, green leaves) isn't finished.
principles.how: Before calling art done, make sure it expresses the light it reflects in its environment, even if lighting is handled by another team member.
principles.anti_pattern: Making the tree and being done with it.
principles.example: A tree with brown trunk and green leaf textures.
principles.quote: Don't draw the asset, draw the light it reflects.

principles.principle: Use colored light, hue variation and atmosphere on repeated assets
principles.why: Colored light creates contrast within a group, slight hue variations add impact because light scatters as it reflects, and atmosphere brings depth and distance.
principles.how: Light groups of copied assets with colored light, brighten spots that get more light, vary hues slightly, and add atmosphere beyond plain fog.
principles.anti_pattern: Copy-pasted identical assets with no variation.
principles.example: A forest of cut-and-pasted trees improved step by step.
principles.quote: Colored light shining down on the scene creates contrast among the group.

principles.principle: Favor cheap techniques so more objects fit on screen
principles.why: Shaders and post-processing can add detail on powerful machines, but that luxury is rare; the less you process an object, the more of it you can put on screen.
principles.how: Achieve lighting and color variation in the asset itself where possible rather than relying on heavy per-object processing.
principles.anti_pattern: Relying on expensive shaders when the hardware budget is tight.
principles.quote: In terms of hardware performance, the less we process an object, the more of it we can put on screen.

summary: When your audience mixes beginners and veterans, layer optional depth on a simple core, as copy abilities sit on top of inhale-and-spit, so novices can finish the game and experts can dig deeper.
takeaways: Copy ability let beginners and veterans both enjoy the game
The game is finishable with just inhale and spit
Copy abilities gave every enemy meaning
Rebalanced overpowered flight through context instead of cutting it
Novice extras were optional, entered from the world map

principles.principle: Layer optional depth over a simple core both audiences can use
principles.why: In a matured NES market with few beginners, he needed to satisfy both beginners and veterans; copy abilities let novices finish with inhale-and-spit while experienced players dig deeper.
principles.how: Build a minimal core that can finish the game, add an optional depth system on top, and verify a core-only playthrough works.
principles.anti_pattern: Requiring the depth system to progress.
principles.example: Kirby's Adventure copy ability.
principles.quote: Players who aren't used to complex game mechanics can finish the game just by inhaling enemies and spitting them out.

principles.principle: Give every enemy a meaning the player looks forward to
principles.why: The copy ability made players look forward to each new enemy encounter, so every individual enemy had meaning, and it boosted Kirby's appeal as a character.
principles.how: Let each enemy type offer something distinct the player can take, such as an ability.
principles.example: Kirby's Adventure copy abilities.
principles.quote: Every individual enemy now had meaning, which was a huge deal.

principles.principle: Rebalance an overpowered ability through context before cutting it
principles.why: More screen space made flight able to bypass nearly any challenge; he considered removing it but instead expanded the info panel, kept mid-boss fights to one screen and reduced flight speed, ending up nicely balanced.
principles.how: Constrain a too-strong mechanic by shrinking play space, confining key fights to one screen, or lowering its speed.
principles.anti_pattern: Cutting a signature mechanic outright.
principles.example: Kirby's Adventure flight and its expanded info panel.
principles.quote: I actually thought about removing flight entirely, but decided against it in the end.

principles.principle: Make novice-friendly extras optional and skippable
principles.why: He added three one-button minigames for novice players, with entrances on the world map so players free to skip them could.
principles.how: Put extras aimed at one audience behind optional entrances on the map rather than in the critical path.
principles.anti_pattern: Forcing extras on players who aren't interested.
principles.example: Kirby's Adventure one-button minigames.
principles.quote: All the fun, none of the complex controls.

summary: Keep idea presentations fast-moving: cut the fat, go straight to the heart of the topic, drop justifications and alternatives, and use simple graphics.
takeaways: Presentations are all about speed
Trim the fat; get to the heart of the topic
Skip justifications and alternatives
Use simple graphics
Not necessarily short, but always moving

principles.principle: Keep presentations fast: go straight to the core idea
principles.why: Creators must communicate their ideas, and his secret to doing it well is speed: trimming the fat and getting right to the heart of the topic.
principles.how: Cut anything not serving the core idea, drop justifications and alternatives, and use simple graphics.
principles.anti_pattern: Long preambles, justifications and lists of alternatives.
principles.quote: Keep those presentations speedy. Trim the fat, and get right to the heart of your topic. Forget justifications or alternatives.

principles.principle: Fill your time, but never let the pace stall
principles.why: A presentation doesn't have to be short; what matters most is keeping things moving and making the most of the time you have.
principles.how: Rehearse for pace rather than brevity, and keep each part moving to the next.
principles.anti_pattern: Confusing speed with cutting the presentation short.
principles.quote: And remember, it doesn't have to be short. Just keep things moving and make the most of the time you have.

summary: Treat awards as a celebration for creators and fans rather than a race, judge each game against its own goals and audience, and value originality, not just sales.
takeaways: The game you like best is number one
Awards celebrate creators and fans; they aren't a race
Raising one game needn't bring others down
Game Designers Award values originality over sales

principles.principle: Judge each game against its own goals and audience
principles.why: Every game has its own values, goals and audience, and diversity is what makes games great, so one style isn't necessarily better than the next.
principles.how: When evaluating a game, ask whether it achieves what it set out to do for its intended players instead of ranking it on one scale.
principles.anti_pattern: Choosing one universal 'best' game.
principles.quote: Every game has its own values, goals, and audience, so the idea of choosing one "best" game isn't something I can really get behind.

principles.principle: Recognize ingenuity, not just commercial success
principles.why: User-vote awards favor games that sold well; directors who know the struggle of making unique games can put ingenuity front and center, which creates possibilities.
principles.how: When judging or recognizing work, include an originality criterion assessed by experienced creators alongside popularity.
principles.anti_pattern: Equating sales or popularity with merit.
principles.example: Japan Game Awards' Game Designers Award, voted by directors of unique games.
principles.quote: For the Game Designers Award, ingenuity—not commercial success— is put front and center by directors who know the struggle of creating unique games.

principles.principle: Celebrate others' success without tearing other games down
principles.why: Awards work best as a way for creators and fans to celebrate and spread happiness; raising one thing up doesn't mean bringing everything around it down.
principles.how: Frame recognition as celebration of the team's hard work and of good games, not as a race.
principles.anti_pattern: Treating awards as a race.
principles.quote: Raising one thing up doesn't mean bringing everything around it down in the process.

summary: Before animation starts, give animators an animation list with every move's length and attack timing (chosen around the game's push and pull) plus photos of a posed figure for key poses, and give direction with all the animators in the room.
takeaways: Start with an animation list: every move, length, attack timing
Choose timings with the game's push and pull in mind
Show key poses with photos of a posed figure
About 70-80 pages of pose images per fighter
Give animation direction with all animators present

principles.principle: Specify every animation's length and attack timing up front
principles.why: Communicating animation ideas to the team is vital, and he sets timings that feel right with the game's push and pull in mind before animators start.
principles.how: Write an animation list describing each movement in text with its length and when the attack occurs; mark loops like idle and walk as 'Loop' or 'Any'.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. fighter animation lists.
principles.quote: I also note animation length, as well as when the attack itself occurs.

principles.principle: Show key poses with photographs of a posed figure
principles.why: Text alone isn't enough for crucial poses like idles, movement and attacks; photographed figure poses make it clear what moves should look like.
principles.how: Pose a figure, photograph it, cut out the shape, adjust contrast and add it to the spec sheet; add source-game screenshots when relevant and use text only for non-humanoid characters.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. spec sheets, 70-80 pages of images per fighter on average.
principles.quote: Take your figure. Photograph it. Cut out the shape. Adjust the contrast.

principles.principle: Give animation direction with all animators present
principles.why: Sharing practical knowledge and pointers with everyone helps the team avoid repeating the same missteps and improves everyone's skills together.
principles.how: Hold feedback sessions with the whole animation team rather than one-on-one.
principles.anti_pattern: Feedback given privately that others never hear.
principles.quote: Whenever I give directions about animation, I make sure all my animators are present.

principles.principle: Let animators fill gaps while keeping the character's appeal first
principles.why: A figure's range of motion is far lower than an in-game model's, so animators must fill gaps and work out details; some ideas don't go as planned and may be let go.
principles.how: Treat the spec as a first step, be willing to drop ideas that don't work, and judge results by whether the character shines.
principles.anti_pattern: Treating the director's spec as the finished animation.
principles.quote: I always take extra care to try and make the character shine and offer the best game experience possible.

summary: Build an RPG's push and pull from exploration (go deeper for bigger rewards at the risk of losing your spoils) and combat (read enemies and exploit their weaknesses), and match the complexity to how casual your game is.
takeaways: Exploration: press your luck deeper or get out
Losing spoils on defeat makes the risk clear
Casual games can raise individual battle difficulty instead
Sizing up and exploiting weaknesses is strategy and game essence
Don't let RPG conventions limit your push and pull

principles.principle: Make going deeper a gamble with spoils at stake
principles.why: In RPG exploration, deeper areas hold stronger enemies but greater rewards, and falling in battle loses the spoils you found, so risk and reward are clear.
principles.how: Scale enemy strength and rewards with dungeon depth and make defeat cost collected spoils so retreating is a real choice.
principles.quote: Do you press your luck? Or get out while you still can?

principles.principle: Offset easy exits with harder individual battles
principles.why: Games that let you exit dungeons at will or skip resource stress are more casual, but raising the difficulty of individual battles keeps a nice balance.
principles.how: If you remove exploration risk, add challenge back into each fight.
principles.anti_pattern: Removing all tension along with the exploration risk.
principles.quote: By increasing the difficulty of individual battles, they can still hit a nice balance.

principles.principle: Telegraph enemy weaknesses and reward exploiting them
principles.why: Players size enemies up by look and behavior; exploiting weaknesses is both strategy and game essence, and Persona's weakness combos add variety and rhythm. Casual games shouldn't get too complex.
principles.how: Give enemies cues that hint at weaknesses and reward exploiting them with extra payoffs like combo setups, scaled to your audience.
principles.anti_pattern: Overly complex weakness systems in casual games.
principles.example: Persona: exploiting weaknesses sets up combos.
principles.quote: Exploiting enemy weaknesses to maximize your damage output— that's both strategy and game essence at play.

summary: Don't rely on additive blending alone; mix crisp shapes and darker elements into your effects so they pop with contrast against any background.
takeaways: Additive blending pushes colors toward white
Additive alone gives decent results, but that's it
Make crisp polygons or simple images the focus
Mix in dark elements for contrast on light backgrounds
Pair opposing elements to make any design stand out

principles.principle: Don't rely on additive blending alone for effects
principles.why: Additive blending pushes colors toward white and gives decent results from simple visuals, but effects then lack impact and contrast and won't stand out on light backgrounds.
principles.how: Use additive layers as support, not the whole effect, and test effects against your brightest backgrounds.
principles.anti_pattern: Keeping the whole game dark just so effects show.
principles.quote: Don't let additive blending do all the work for you!

principles.principle: Make crisp shapes the focal point of each effect
principles.why: Adding polygons or simple images and making them the focus gives effects pop; Smash Ultimate does this with all its effects for a clean, anime-style look.
principles.how: Build each effect around solid polygons or simple images, with glow around them.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate effects.
principles.quote: Try adding polygons or simple images to your carefully-crafted effect and making those the focus.

principles.principle: Mix dark elements into effects for contrast
principles.why: Effects often look too bright in a scene; darker elements make them visible against light backgrounds.
principles.how: Add darker elements to bright-only effects, and more broadly pair opposites, like straight lines in a curvy design.
principles.anti_pattern: Effects built only from bright elements.
principles.example: Before/after effect samples.
principles.quote: With any kind of design—not just effects—it's best to think about how opposing elements might help your imagery stand out.

summary: Make players understand why your game is fun within the first three minutes by getting to real gameplay fast, in both your trailers and your opening, and saving long story and CG for later.
takeaways: Show why the game is fun within three minutes
Trailers should reach gameplay quickly; save CG for later
Long prologues start a game on the wrong foot
RPGs can open with a later slice of action
Weave tutorials into the main game, and make them fun

principles.principle: Make the fun clear within the first three minutes
principles.why: From the arcade world: players quickly judge whether a game is fun, and if you make them wait too long they may put it down.
principles.how: Time your opening so a new player is playing and understands the core fun within three minutes.
principles.anti_pattern: Slow starts.
principles.example: Arcade games.
principles.quote: Players should understand why a game is fun in the first three minutes.

principles.principle: Open on gameplay, not long prologues
principles.why: Long prologues just delay players from playing; even RPGs that need introduction should lay things out so gameplay comes first.
principles.how: Start with a playable slice from later in the story, or a battle as non-protagonist characters, and save story setup for later.
principles.anti_pattern: Opening with long prologues.
principles.quote: A game that starts slow is often a game that's starting on the wrong foot.

principles.principle: Show real gameplay early in trailers
principles.why: Many trailers open with long story sequences and he skips ahead; people can't be expected to buy a game if they can't tell what kind of game it is.
principles.how: Put gameplay footage near the start and save high-end CG movies and openings for later.
principles.anti_pattern: Trailers that open with story.
principles.example: Game trailers on online storefronts.
principles.quote: Save the high-end CG movies and openings for later.

principles.principle: Weave fun tutorials into the main game
principles.why: Video is something other media can do, so give players a taste of the fun only games offer; tutorials should be fun too.
principles.how: Integrate teaching into real play instead of separate, obvious practice sessions.
principles.anti_pattern: Tutorials that feel like obvious practice.
principles.quote: Tutorials should be fun, too. Don't make them obvious practice, but instead try to weave them more naturally into the main game.

summary: Treat clarity and style in UI as a trade-off you settle per game: organize menus like a tidy drawer, fit the style to your game's content and setting, and make things as user-friendly as you can.
takeaways: Clarity and style in UI are arguably contradictory
Clear UI isn't always good UI, or vice versa
A UI is like a drawer: organize it sensibly
Check guidance, size, hierarchy, brightness, saturation, typeface
Fit UI to the game's content and setting

principles.principle: Choose the clarity-style balance to fit your game
principles.why: Persona's UI is the most stylish but hard to parse, yet traditional menus would be unwanted; clear UI doesn't always mean good UI, so it depends on what each title demands.
principles.how: Decide early where your UI sits between clarity and style based on the game's content and setting, then improve user-friendliness where you can.
principles.anti_pattern: Assuming the clearest UI is automatically best.
principles.example: Persona series / Persona 5 menus.
principles.quote: In other words, clear UI doesn't always mean good UI, or vice-versa.

principles.principle: Organize menus like a sensible drawer
principles.why: When players pull a menu open they want things organized sensibly; feature-heavy games need drawers on top of drawers, and crafting games leave players drowning in materials.
principles.how: Group related items and plan a window hierarchy proportional to the amount of content and items.
principles.example: Minecraft players build warehouses like their own item folders.
principles.quote: A game's UI is like a drawer. When you pull it open, you want things to be organized in a sensible way.

principles.principle: Review every menu's guidance, size, hierarchy, color and typeface
principles.why: Each menu has key design points: visual guidance, size of display elements, window hierarchy, brightness and saturation, and an appropriate typeface.
principles.how: Use those points as a checklist when designing or reviewing each menu.

summary: Use what happens on screen (movement speed, inertia, jump physics, lag, frame rate) to decide how "heavy" or "light" the same physical button feels, and give each character its own distinct weight.
takeaways: On-screen response makes the same button feel light or heavy
Speed, inertia, jump physics, lag, frame rate affect weight
Players feel feedback through their hands
Distinct fighter weights create push and pull
Configure analog tilt sensitivity for each console

principles.principle: Tune on-screen response to set how heavy buttons feel
principles.why: The same button press can feel light or heavy depending on movement speed, inertia, jump physics, lag and frame rate; players somehow feel feedback with their hands.
principles.how: Decide each character's intended weight and tune speed, inertia and jump physics to it, counting lag and frame rate as part of feel.
principles.anti_pattern: Assuming feel comes only from physical hardware.
principles.example: NES control pad games that feel radically different.
principles.quote: Even with the same button presses, the response you see on-screen can make them feel so very different.

principles.principle: Differentiate characters by speed, vulnerability and animation flair
principles.why: Differences in movement speed, vulnerability and animation flair create the push and pull of versus matches and make characters feel wildly different in your hands.
principles.how: Give each playable character a distinct mix of speed, vulnerability and animation style.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. fighters.
principles.quote: Not only does this create the "push and pull" that makes for a fun versus match, it also makes for characters that feel wildly different in your hands.

principles.principle: Configure analog stick tilt sensitivity per console
principles.why: Each console's analog stick is slightly different, so the lowest value at which tilt is detected must be configured every time.
principles.how: Set and test the minimum detected stick tilt separately for each platform or controller you support.
principles.anti_pattern: One stick-sensitivity value for every console.
principles.quote: Tilt sensitivity— the lowest value at which stick tilt is detected— is something we have to configure every time.

summary: Meet hard requests with structural ideas, as Kirby Super Star made co-op work by splitting players into a lead and a Helper and offered lots of content without wearing players out by packaging short, distinct scenarios as an "omnibus."
takeaways: Helper system: camera follows lead; off-screen partner Space Jumps back
Enemies became playable Helpers via copy abilities
More moves per ability meant enemies needed more hits
Omnibus of short scenarios avoids fatigue with one style
Unfamiliar CG backgrounds fit Kirby poorly, but skills grew

principles.principle: In co-op scrollers, let the camera follow one lead player
principles.why: In side-scrollers players pull each other along as they scroll, which breaks down with jumping and with copy abilities moving at very different speeds; focusing the screen on one lead solved it.
principles.how: Make one player the camera's lead and warp any supporting player who drifts too far off-screen back to them.
principles.anti_pattern: Letting all players scroll the screen with equal weight.
principles.example: Kirby Super Star Helper system and Space Jump.
principles.quote: Instead of letting both characters scroll the screen with equal weight, I placed the focus on only the lead character.

principles.principle: Raise enemy durability when moves gain variety and strength
principles.why: Copy abilities gained many moves via repeat presses, directional inputs and commands; enemies that survive a few hits let stronger moves set abilities apart.
principles.how: When adding moves of differing power, make standard enemies take several hits so strength differences show.
principles.anti_pattern: One-hit enemies that make every move equal.
principles.example: Kirby Super Star copy abilities vs. Kirby's Adventure's one move per ability.
principles.quote: To compensate, we gave even standard enemies the ability to survive a few hits.

principles.principle: Deliver volume as short, distinct scenarios to avoid fatigue
principles.why: Too many games took too long to beat; an omnibus of quick-to-beat scenarios, each with its own gameplay, gives lots of content without tiring players of one style.
principles.how: Split content into short, self-contained modes with their own rules and themes, chosen from a hub, and keep each one distinct.
principles.anti_pattern: Scenarios that play the same, like Spring Breeze once copy abilities were added.
principles.example: Kirby Super Star omnibus cork board.
principles.quote: I thought I could provide a lot of content without causing players to grow tired of any one style.

principles.principle: Check a new production technique fits before adopting it mid-project
principles.why: Kirby Super Star switched to CG backgrounds mid-development following the Donkey Kong Country trend; the staff weren't familiar with it and it didn't fit Kirby's pieced-together terrain, though learning new skills still matters.
principles.how: Before adopting a trendy technique, confirm the team knows it and it suits how levels are built; treat it as skill-building if you proceed.
principles.anti_pattern: Following an art trend that doesn't fit your game.
principles.example: Kirby Super Star CG backgrounds.
principles.quote: Still, it's important to learn new skills. The things you make today can lead to what you make tomorrow.

summary: Design for the player's experience, not the developers' convenience, because players won't cut you slack for a hard development, and when a compromise would hurt players, look for alternatives with your programmers.
takeaways: Specs often prioritize developers' jobs over player experience
Players won't cut you slack because development was hard
You're doing this for the player and nobody else
Find alternatives with programmers: ideal versus feasible

principles.principle: Put player experience ahead of development convenience in specs
principles.why: Design documents often come back prioritizing the developers' jobs; sometimes that's a sensible efficiency compromise, but players only care whether the game is good and won't cut you slack.
principles.how: Flag every spec decision made for convenience and keep it only if players won't suffer for it.
principles.anti_pattern: Specs that prioritize ease of development over the player.
principles.example: A designer's design document.
principles.quote: Players aren't concerned about why developers do what they do. They only care if a game is good or not.

principles.principle: When a compromise would hurt players, look for other solutions
principles.why: Issues, varied tastes and technical limits are unavoidable, but you're making the game for the player and nobody else; developers are players too and should know how customers feel.
principles.how: Before accepting a player-unfriendly compromise, search for alternative solutions.
principles.anti_pattern: Expecting players to forgive problems caused by hard development.
principles.quote: But when push comes to shove, you're doing this for the player, and nobody else.

principles.principle: Balance ideal and feasible together with your programmers
principles.why: This isn't just a design issue; you need to strike a balance between what's ideal and what's technologically feasible.
principles.how: Bring programmers into discussions about compromises early to find feasible ways to keep the player experience.
principles.quote: Talk to your programmers, too. In the end, you'll need to strike a balance between what's ideal and what's technologically feasible.

summary: Name development files and labels with a consistent, concise scheme that stays tidy when sorted (category first, then direction, then numbers for strength), so anyone can tell what a file is at a glance.
takeaways: Every Smash action has a logical file label
Category first, then direction, then strength numbers
Names should sort neatly and read at a glance
In-game names follow the player's input order
Avoid romanized Japanese in file names

principles.principle: Order name parts so sorting groups related files
principles.why: With 'Attack' or 'Special' first and numbers for strength, moves stay together sorted from neutral to tilt to smash; direction-first names like 'SAttack' or word-based strengths would make a mess when sorted.
principles.how: Use category, then direction (N/Hi/S/Lw, Air), then numbers for strength or sequence, and check folders sort sensibly.
principles.anti_pattern: Putting modifiers before the category, or using words for strength.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. labels: Attack11-13, AttackS4, AttackAirF, SpecialHi.
principles.quote: If we called them "SAttack" or "HiAttack," with the direction coming first... It would just make a huge mess when you sorted them all.

principles.principle: Keep labels concise but readable at a glance
principles.why: Someone seeing a name for the first time should know what it's for; names that are too short are easy to type but hard to understand.
principles.how: Pick names that balance brevity with clarity, and test them on someone new to the project.
principles.anti_pattern: Cryptic abbreviations.
principles.quote: Keep your development file names and labels concise and easy to understand!

principles.principle: Avoid romanized native-language words in shared file names
principles.why: On bigger projects, romanized Japanese makes things harder for people who don't speak the language, and overseas teams joining later may not understand it.
principles.how: Name files in English whenever other or international teams might work on the project.
principles.anti_pattern: Romanized Japanese file names.
principles.quote: Remember: it's not just you who needs to understand your game.

principles.principle: Name player-facing moves in the order players input them
principles.why: In-game it's 'Up Special' because from the player's perspective the directional input comes first, so the name matches how you perform the move.
principles.how: Let in-game move names follow the input sequence, even if internal labels follow a different scheme.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. 'Up Special' vs. internal 'SpecialHi'.
principles.quote: The name matches how you perform the move.

summary: Keep the next reward visible and within reach by showing how far players have come and how far they have left, so they always have a clear objective pulling them forward.
takeaways: Keep the next reward in sight to motivate players
Show current progress and what's needed to reach it
Few expensive, powerful items make saving up a goal
Generous money and lots of gear weaken this effect

principles.principle: Show progress toward the next reward and what remains
principles.why: Ys displays current EXP and the amount needed to level up; the number rising with each defeated enemy shows how far you've come and how far is left, which keeps you pushing.
principles.how: Display current versus required values for the next reward on the main screen and update them on every gain.
principles.anti_pattern: Hiding how close the player is to the next reward.
principles.example: Ys (TurboGrafx-16 version) EXP display.
principles.quote: It shows how far you've come, and how far you have left to go. Keeping rewards in sight.

principles.principle: Always keep a clear, reachable objective in front of players
principles.why: Keeping rewards in sight and providing a clear objective both motivate players; it's a shame when a game doesn't keep you thinking about the next reward.
principles.how: Check at points throughout a playthrough what the player is working toward, and add nearer objectives where it's unclear.
principles.quote: I do think it's a shame when a game doesn't keep you thinking about the next reward.

principles.principle: Make key purchases scarce, costly and powerful
principles.why: In Faxanadu, a few expensive items that give a massive boost make players scrounge for money and plan toward the next gear; generous money and lots of equipment make this fun harder to provide.
principles.how: Limit shop items to a few high-impact pieces priced so saving for them is a goal.
principles.anti_pattern: Flooding players with money and minor gear.
principles.example: Faxanadu shops.
principles.quote: The player scrounges for money, thinking about how much more they need for the next big piece of gear— a real plus for the game.
